# Mine

A set of small PWAs that keep your personal data as markdown in a private GitHub repo —
calendar, zettelkasten, diary — so it stays portable and free of vendor lock-in.

**Live: https://maximilianharr.github.io/mine/** — install it to your home screen.

## Docs

| | |
| --- | --- |
| [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md) | what the app does and how it behaves |
| [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) | how it is built, and the verified platform findings |
| [TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md](TEST-REQUIREMENTS.md) | what is checked before a change ships, and how |
| [calendar/](calendar/) | the calendar app, with its own pair of docs |

## Layout

```
style.css                                         the shared base: tokens and chrome
index.html app.js home.css sw.js manifest.json    the main app
shared/   apps.js store.js github.js md.js        used by every app
          markdown.js prefs.js ui.js sync.js
          vendor/
calendar/                                         one folder per app
spike/                                            on-device platform checks
test/                                             the checks: test/run.sh
```

No build step: no bundler, no CI, no dependencies to install. `git push` deploys to GitHub
Pages. To run it locally, `python3 -m http.server` in this folder and open the printed URL.
`test/run.sh` runs the model checks in node and the rest in a headless browser, and installs
nothing either.

Data lives in a **separate private repo**, never in this one. The token is entered once in the
app, stored on the device, and scoped so it can only touch that data repo.

## Status

The main app, the sync layer and the on-device checks are done and verified end to end against a
real repo. The calendar is built — the five views, the kanban, the entry popup and its field
popups, the filter and the settings — and `test/run.sh` covers it.

Not built yet: the per-app summary above the tiles that [REQUIREMENTS.md](REQUIREMENTS.md)
describes. The tile screen shows tiles only, so opening the calendar is currently the only way
to see what is on today.

=== calendar/sample/2026/04/2026-04-18-1400-k3f9.md
---
title: "Project Phoenix: Weekly Sync"
type: event
start: 2026-04-18T14:00:00Z
end: 2026-04-18T15:00:00Z
group: work
location: "Virtual / Conference Room 3B"
alerts:
  - 0
  - 15
participants:
  - "jane.doe@example.com"
  - "john.smith@example.com"
---

# Agenda: Project Phoenix Sync

This meeting is for the weekly alignment on the Project Phoenix initiative. Please come
prepared to discuss your progress and any blockers.
=== calendar/sample/2026/04/2026-04-20-0000-t2wv.md
---
title: "Draft the Q2 hiring plan"
type: task
start: 2026-04-20
stage: doing
important: true
estimate: 3
group: work
participants:
  - "jane.doe@example.com"
---

A task carries the three keys an event never has: `stage`, `important` and `estimate`.

- `stage` is `todo`, `doing` or `done` and is the only record of progress - there is no
  `done` flag.
- `important` is a plain yes or no, and only `true` is ever written: a task that is not
  important carries no key at all. There is no priority scale and no `priority` key.
- `estimate` is in days. It has no RFC 5545 equivalent, so the name is ours.

There is no `sprint` key. The sprint is whichever range in `settings.md` this `start` falls
in, so the number can never disagree with the date, and moving the card to another sprint is
exactly a change of `start`. With the anchor and interval in `sample/settings.md` this one is
in sprint 8, 13-26 April 2026.
=== calendar/sample/2026/04/2026-04-25-0000-ov1q.md
---
series: trash-p7qm
recurrence-id: 2026-04-25
stage: done
---

Override for a single occurrence of `recurring/trash-p7qm.md`: this one week is ticked
off. Only the keys that differ from the series are present; everything else is inherited.
Moving a single occurrence works the same way, by setting `start` here.
=== calendar/sample/recurring/trash-p7qm.md
---
title: "take out the trash"
type: task
start: 2026-04-18
stage: todo
group: home
recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=SA"
exdate:
  - 2026-05-02
alerts:
  - 0
---

- Put trashcan next to street with handlebar facing towards the street
- Make sure to clean trashcan afterwards
=== calendar/sample/groups.md
---
groups:
  work:   { color: "#c0392b", label: "Work" }
  home:   { color: "#27ae60", label: "Household" }
  health: { color: "#2980b9", label: "Sport & Doctor" }
---

Maps an entry's `group` name to a colour and a label. Editing a colour here recolours
every entry in that group; no entry files are touched.
=== calendar/sample/settings.md
---
kanban-anchor: 2026-01-05
kanban-interval: 2
---

The two calendar settings that are data rather than preferences.

`kanban-anchor` is a bare date: the first day of sprint 1. `kanban-interval` is the sprint
length in weeks. Sprint *n* therefore runs for `interval` weeks from
`anchor + (n-1) x interval` weeks, and a task's sprint is whichever range its `start` falls
in.

They live in the repo because the sprint is *derived* from them. On the device the same file
would report a different sprint on a phone than on a laptop, and moving a card would then
write the wrong date. Everything else - theme, date format, time zone, week start,
show-calendar-weeks, the group filter - is a device preference and is not in the repo.

A `start` before the anchor has no sprint, and such a task is not on the board.

#!/bin/bash
# Runs the model checks in node, then starts the fixture server and a headless Chromium for the
# browser checks and tears both down.
#
#   test/run.sh              every check
#   test/run.sh --shot DIR   every check, and a screenshot of each view into DIR
#   test/run.sh mine         one app's browser checks, by the name in test/check-<app>.mjs
#
# Needs chromium and node 20+ on PATH. Nothing is installed and nothing is written to the repo.
#
# A browser suite per app, discovered rather than listed: adding test/check-diary.mjs is all it
# takes for the diary to be checked by this script. They share one Chromium and run in turn,
# because they drive the same page target.
set -u
HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
PORT=8787
PROFILE=$(mktemp -d)

cleanup() {
  [ -n "${CHROME:-}" ] && kill "$CHROME" 2>/dev/null
  [ -n "${SERVER:-}" ] && kill "$SERVER" 2>/dev/null
  rm -rf "$PROFILE" 2>/dev/null
  return 0
}
trap cleanup EXIT

command -v chromium >/dev/null || { echo "chromium not on PATH"; exit 2; }

# A bare word is an app name; everything else is passed to the suites.
ONLY=""
ARGS=()
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --shot) ARGS+=("$1" "$2"); shift 2 ;;
    -*) ARGS+=("$1"); shift ;;
    *) ONLY="$1"; shift ;;
  esac
done

SUITES=()
for f in "$HERE"/check-*.mjs; do
  name=$(basename "$f" .mjs); name=${name#check-}
  [ -n "$ONLY" ] && [ "$ONLY" != "$name" ] && continue
  SUITES+=("$f")
done
if [ ${#SUITES[@]} -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "no browser suite matches '${ONLY}' — expected test/check-${ONLY}.mjs"
  exit 2
fi

node "$HERE/unit.mjs" || exit 1

python3 "$HERE/serve.py" $PORT >/dev/null 2>&1 &
SERVER=$!
chromium --headless --no-sandbox --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --no-first-run \
  --disable-extensions --remote-debugging-port=9222 --user-data-dir="$PROFILE" \
  about:blank >/dev/null 2>&1 &
CHROME=$!

for i in $(seq 30); do
  curl -sf -o /dev/null "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/calendar/" && break
  sleep 0.2
done

# Node 20 keeps WebSocket behind a flag; 21+ ignores the flag harmlessly.
failed=0
for suite in "${SUITES[@]}"; do
  node --experimental-websocket "$suite" ${ARGS[@]+"${ARGS[@]}"} 2>&1 \
    | grep -v 'ExperimentalWarning\|Use `node'
  [ "${PIPESTATUS[0]}" -eq 0 ] || failed=1
done
exit $failed
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Serves the working tree for the browser checks, plus one synthetic route per app.

/__fixture/<app>.json is what test/check-<app>.mjs seeds the local mirror with. It is generated
rather than committed as markdown so that it always lands in the month the checks run in - a
fixture pinned to April would leave the month view empty and the checks green.

A new app adds a function here and names it in FIXTURES. An app with no data of its own - the
tile screen - takes the empty one, which still gets it a config and a mirror to open against.
"""
import http.server, json, os, sys
from datetime import date

REPO = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
PORT = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 8787

# Weekday offsets within the month, so there is always a Saturday task, a day with more entries
# than a phone cell shows, all-day items, and the long titles that used to blow the grid open.
#
# A task row may carry a sixth item: extra frontmatter lines - `important: true` for the
# importance checks, a recurrence rule for the repeating ones.
ROWS = [
    (1,  "09:00", "Sprint planning",                  "work",   "event"),
    (1,  "14:00", "Review the open pull requests",    "work",   "task",  "todo",
     ["important: true"]),
    (2,  None,    "Dentist",                          "health", "event"),
    (3,  "08:30", "Standup",                          "work",   "event"),
    (3,  "11:00", "Write the quarterly board report", "work",   "task",  "doing"),
    (3,  "17:00", "Gym",                              "health", "event"),
    (5,  "13:00", "Deploy the release",               "work",   "task",  "todo"),
    (3,  None,    "Water the plants",                 "home",   "task",  "todo",
     ['recurrence: "FREQ=WEEKLY"']),
    (6,  "10:00", "Fix the bathroom tap",             "home",   "task",  "todo"),
    (7,  None,    "Family lunch",                     "home",   "event"),
    (10, "08:30", "Standup",                          "work",   "event"),
    (12, "11:00", "Weekly shop",                      "home",   "task",  "done"),
    (15, "14:00", "Physiotherapy appointment",        "health", "event"),
    (17, "10:00", "Architecture review",              "work",   "event"),
    (17, "16:00", "Call the insurance company",       "home",   "task",  "todo"),
    (20, "09:00", "Design review",                    "work",   "event"),
    (20, "15:00", "Submit the expenses",              "work",   "task",  "todo",
     ["important: true"]),
    (21, "10:00", "Repaint the hallway",              "home",   "task",  "todo"),
    (24, "13:00", "Doctor",                           "health", "event"),
    (26, "09:00", "Sprint review",                    "work",   "event"),
]


def calendar():
    today = date.today()
    files = [
        {"path": "calendar/groups.md", "oid": "g1",
         "text": open(os.path.join(REPO, "calendar/sample/groups.md")).read()},
        {"path": "calendar/settings.md", "oid": "s1",
         "text": "---\nkanban-anchor: %s\nkanban-interval: 2\n---\n" % today.replace(day=1)},
    ]
    for i, row in enumerate(ROWS):
        day, time, title, group, kind = row[:5]
        key = "%04d-%02d-%02d" % (today.year, today.month, day)
        fm = ['title: "%s"' % title, "type: " + kind]
        if time:
            fm.append("start: %sT%s:00Z" % (key, time))
            fm.append("end: %sT%02d:%s:00Z" % (key, int(time[:2]) + 1, time[3:]))
        else:
            fm.append("start: " + key)
        fm.append("group: " + group)
        if kind == "task":
            fm.append("stage: " + row[5])
        fm.extend(row[6] if len(row) > 6 else [])
        files.append({
            "path": "calendar/%04d/%02d/%s-%s-%04x.md" % (
                today.year, today.month, key, (time or "0000").replace(":", ""), i),
            "oid": "f%d" % i,
            "text": "---\n" + "\n".join(fm) + "\n---\n\nNotes for %s.\n" % title})
    return files


# The tile screen reads no files of its own: what it needs is the config the seed writes anyway.
FIXTURES = {"calendar": calendar, "mine": lambda: []}

def calendar():
    today = date.today()
    files = [
        {"path": "calendar/groups.md", "oid": "g1",
         "text": open(os.path.join(REPO, "calendar/sample/groups.md")).read()},
        {"path": "calendar/settings.md", "oid": "s1",
         "text": "---\nkanban-anchor: %s\nkanban-interval: 2\n---\n" % today.replace(day=1)},
    ]
    for i, row in enumerate(ROWS):
        day, time, title, group, kind = row[:5]
        key = "%04d-%02d-%02d" % (today.year, today.month, day)
        fm = ['title: "%s"' % title, "type: " + kind]
        if time:
            fm.append("start: %sT%s:00Z" % (key, time))
            fm.append("end: %sT%02d:%s:00Z" % (key, int(time[:2]) + 1, time[3:]))
        else:
            fm.append("start: " + key)
        fm.append("group: " + group)
        if kind == "task":
            fm.append("stage: " + row[5])
        fm.extend(row[6] if len(row) > 6 else [])
        files.append({
            "path": "calendar/%04d/%02d/%s-%s-%04x.md" % (
                today.year, today.month, key, (time or "0000").replace(":", ""), i),
            "oid": "f%d" % i,
            "text": "---\n" + "\n".join(fm) + "\n---\n\nNotes for %s.\n" % title})
    return files

# Calendar

Calendar is an app of [Mine](../REQUIREMENTS.md) to manage your calendar. Every entry is one
markdown file in the data repo, so your calendar stays readable and portable without this app.

See [TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md](TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md) for the file format.

## What an entry holds

A title, a type — **event** or **task** — a start and end, a group, a location, participants,
alerts, and a free markdown body for the agenda, checklist or notes.

A task also carries a **stage** — `todo`, `doing` or `done` — and, optionally, an **important**
mark and an estimate in days. An event has none of the three. Stage is the only record of a
task's progress; there is no separate done flag.

**Important is a plain yes or no, not a scale.** There is no priority 1, 2 and 3. Three tiers
asked you to decide twice — once whether a task matters and again how much — and the second
answer never changed what got done first. A task that matters carries `important: true`; a task
that does not carries no key at all, which is the convention the estimate already follows.

A new task starts at `todo` with an estimate of **1 day**. Both are only defaults: either can be
changed before saving, and the estimate can be cleared away again, so `estimate` stays a key an
entry may simply not have — nothing writes one into a task that never carried one.

Entries can repeat, and a repeating entry can have single occurrences skipped, moved, retitled
or moved to another stage without affecting the rest.

## Layout

## Views

- **Year** — every month, each with a weekday header row and one row per week. The current day
  is highlighted. A day with entries takes the background colour of its group, split between
  colours if there are several — a year grid has no room for anything else. Clicking a day shows
  that day's entries, as a preview like everywhere else. **The month's name is a button**: it
  reads as a caption but is pressable, with a hover and a press state, and clicking it opens that
  month in the month view — landing on the month you pointed at rather than the one the anchor is
  in. The whole label is the target, so it stays finger-sized where a day in a year grid is not.

  **At most six months to a row.** The months reflow with the width — four, three, two as it
  narrows — but never more than six, so a year reads as two even rows of six rather than as ten
  and then two. Now that the window is as wide as the browser, the extra width goes into wider
  months with readable day cells; a grid free to keep adding columns spends it on more of them
  instead, and twelve does not divide by seven, eight or ten.
- **Month** — one row per week, and the grid **fills the whole height of the window** below the
  pane: the week rows divide the space between them equally, so the month is as tall as the
  screen allows rather than as tall as its cells happen to need. The extra height goes to the
  cell, **not to more entry lines** — the cap below is about what a glance can read, not about
  what fits. Entries appear inside each day cell as small lines carrying the
  title on the group's background colour, sorted by time, all-day items first. On desktop a timed
  entry's line is prefixed with its time; on a phone it is the title alone, because seven columns
  across a phone have no room for both and the title is the part worth reading — the time is one
  tap away in the day preview. A cell shows at most four on desktop and two on a phone, then
  `+N`. A line is a single line of text: a title too long for the cell is **clipped at the
  cell's edge with no `…`**, because three dots cost three characters in the one place in the app
  where characters are scarcest, and a clipped word already says there is more. The month view
  carries **no done-rectangle** — that width goes to the title; one-tap done stays in the week
  and day grids and in the day preview, and a task seen in the month is moved through its popup
  or on the board. Clicking empty space in a cell creates an entry; clicking an entry opens it.
- **Week** — columns are the days, rows are the 24 hours.
- **Day** — the week view for a single day, with more detail per entry, and **with no day header
  row**. The weekday and the date are already the period label in the top pane, and `TUE 20`
  repeated directly beneath that label was the same fact twice in the one view where there is
  only one day to name. So the day view is the all-day strip and the hour grid, with nothing
  above them. The week view keeps its seven headers: those name seven different days, and the
  pane names none of them.
- **Kanban** — below.

Groups switched off in the filter are not shown in any view.

### The day preview

Clicking a day opens that day's entries as a list, each one tappable. Its top right carries a
small `+` to add an entry on that day and a small `x` to close it — not full-width buttons. It
is reached from a day in the year grid, from a day cell in the month view on a phone, and from
a day header in the week grid. The day view has no header to reach it from, and needs none: it
is already showing the one day the preview would list.

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so do
the settings panel and the day preview. Nothing rises from the bottom edge any more. A centred
card is reached with either thumb and does not pretend to be a drawer that can be dragged. The

content.content:
## Entry popup

The popup **opens in the middle of the screen**, on a phone as much as on a desktop — and so do
the settings panel and the day preview. Nothing rises from the bottom edge any more. A centred
card is reached with either thumb and does not pretend to be a drawer that can be dragged. The
hamburger's menu and the filter hang off the hamburger instead, as dropdowns, and a field's own
popup hangs off its row; those three name the thing they came from, which a centred card cannot.

**There is one popup, and it is both.** Clicking an entry — in any grid, in the day preview, or
as a card on the board — opens the entry, shown as text, and **every value in it is edited where
it is read**: click the thing, change it, and one save at the top writes the lot. There is no
pen, no second popup behind one, and no mode to be in.

It was two before, a read-only preview with a pen into a form, and the reason was sound: a form
answers *what day is this on* in input boxes, which are harder to read than text and leave every
value one slip away from a tap meant to scroll. Editing in place keeps that — a row is text until
it is clicked, so there is still nothing to slip into — and gives back the two things the split
cost. A change was four taps before the field was even typed into: open, pen, row, and back. And
the preview and the
form had to agree about every field twice over, in two blocks of code, which is how one of them
came to show the stage and the other to hide it.

**Each row is edited in place, and one save writes.** The rows hold a draft; nothing reaches the
repo until the popup's own disk, so **one entry edit is one commit** and the popup is one
transaction rather than a stream of them. A row that writes the file the moment it is saved was
tried on paper and gives this popup three faults it cannot see: the entry it is holding goes a
generation stale after the first write, a saved date moves the file out from under it, and four
rows saved offline queue four writes to one path. One save at the end has none of them.

**The disk appears only once something differs from the file**, and it is the only button in the
popup that writes. A popup opened to read has no save in it to wonder about — which is most
openings — and a save that is there is a save with something to do.

```
[☑]                                  [trash] [x]      opened, nothing changed
[☑]                          [trash] [disk] [x]       a row has been changed
[☑] [📅]                             [disk] [x]       a new one: the type is still a choice,
                                                      and the disk is disabled until it has a title
[☑] [this|all]               [trash] [disk] [x]       a repeating one: the scope pair
```

The top row carries **the type**, then right-aligned a trashcan to delete the entry, the disk
once there is something to save, and an `x` to close. On an entry that already exists the type is
a **marker, not a choice** — a ticked square for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and
not pressable — because a task turned into an event drops its stage, its importance and its
estimate, and the type is settled when the entry is made. On a new entry it is the pair, with the
event selected. On a repeating one the **scope pair** follows the marker, left of the gap —
described below.

The trashcan stays at the left of that group: deleting is not an edit of a field, it writes at
once whatever the draft holds, and the board's rule that a card is deleted from its popup in two
taps depends on the trashcan being on the first of them.

Below the row, in this order: the **title**, the **when**, the **toggle row**, the **five field
rows**, and the **details body** last. Nothing about repeating is among them.

### A row, and a row being edited

Every row is **the icon, then the value** — no field name beside it:

```
[ball]    Work                                      [trash]
[pin]     Conference room 3B                        [trash]
[repeat]  Repeat
[bell]    Alerts
```

The name is gone because it said the same thing as the icon it sat beside, in the one column
where the value has to fit. **An unset row shows the field's name in its place, muted** — which
is what an empty input does everywhere else in Mine, and what keeps a bell from being a bell and
nothing else. A set row reads as a value; an unset one reads as an invitation.

- **The rows never move.** Every row is in the canonical order below whether it is set or not.
  Set rows used to be lifted to the top, which moved a row the moment it was filled — so the
  field just typed into was no longer where it had just been looked for. That is the same
  complaint as a row that grows, and it has the same answer: the popup's shape does not depend
  on what is in it.
- **A set row carries a trashcan at its right**, which clears that field in the draft. An unset
  row has nothing to clear and carries none.
- **Opening a row does not change its height.** This is the rule the rest of this section serves.
  A row that grew a heading and a control beneath it moved every row under it, so a popup opened
  to type one word rearranged itself and the eye had to find the field again. Every row is the
  height of the tallest thing a row can hold — its trashcan and its `x`, which a set row already
  carries shut — and nothing a row opens is taller than that.
- **A field whose control fits a line holds it in the line.** The title, the location, the alerts
  and the participants become an input where their value was, at the same size, **with the field's
  name as the placeholder rather than a heading above it**: a heading was the line the row grew
  by, and it named what the icon beside it already said. The trashcan and the `x` stay at the
  right of that same line, where the closed row's trashcan already was, so the way out of a row is
  in the corner it is in everywhere in Mine. **The title row is the one with neither**, because an
  entry must have a title and so there is nothing to clear, and because the popup's own `x`, which
  discards the whole edit, is a thumb's width above that line; it closes on Escape or by opening
  any other row.
- **A field whose control cannot fit a line opens it in a popup anchored to the row.** The when,
  the category, the repetition and the estimate: four date and time boxes, a list of categories, a
  rule with an end condition, a number with a unit. The row keeps its icon, its value and its
  trashcan — **nothing about it moves** — and the popup hangs directly under it, naming the field
  and carrying an `x`. The estimate's is the one that also carries the trashcan, because its row
  is an icon on the toggle row with no room beside it.
- **The field popup carries no scrim**, alone among the calendar's overlays. A scrim would stop
  the tap that dismisses it, so moving from one field to the next would take two taps; without one
  the tap reaches the row it landed on and opens it. Tapping the row it is already on closes it
  rather than reopening it.
- **The `x` closes the row and keeps what is in it.** There is nothing to accept: the editor has
  been writing into the draft since the first keystroke, which is what lets the disk appear the
  moment something differs from the file. So closing a row is only closing it — a field typed
  into is not undone by leaving it, which is what a tap meant for the row below would otherwise
  do. Clearing the field is the trashcan beside the `x`, and undoing the edit of a whole entry is
  the popup's own `x`. There is exactly one save in this popup and it is the one in the top row.
- **Enter closes the row, and only the row.** It used to submit the form, so the key that ended
  a word saved the entry and left for the calendar — the one gesture a popup opened to type one
  word must not make. It closes the row like the row's own `x`, keeping what is in it, and the
  disk in the top row stays the only thing that writes. **Shift+Enter is left alone**, which is
  what puts a new line in the details textarea. Inside a field's own popup Enter is not the row's
  Enter and does nothing: that popup closes by its `x` or by Escape.
- **There is no keyboard save.** The disk is a button in the top row, reached by Tab and pressed
  by Enter or space like any other. A shortcut that wrote and closed would be the thing Enter was
  just stopped from doing, under a different key.
- **Only one row is open at a time**, and a line's input and a field's popup are never both open.
  Opening either closes the other, which likewise keeps what is in it.
- **Escape unwinds the one layer there is.** A field popup swallows it, so Escape inside a field
  does not throw away the edit the field is part of. **An inline row does not** — it is the row in
  its editing state rather than a layer over anything, and leaving it loses nothing, so Escape
  there keeps meaning *leave the popup*. A new entry opens with its title row already an input,
  and making that swallow the first press would cost two presses to leave the commonest popup in
  the app. The row's own `x` is what closes a row.
- **Clicking a row's trashcan does not activate the row.** This is the rule a kanban card already
  holds to, and it matters more here, because the trashcan now sits on the surface being tapped.
  The row and its controls are one place where a click that does two things is easy to build.

**Five of the six fields are rows**, in this canonical order:

- a ball for **category**;
- circular arrows for **repetition**;
- a bell for **alerts**;
- a pin for **location**;
- a person for **participants**.

The sixth, **details**, is not a row: it is the body, and it is drawn in full at the foot of the
popup — described below. A markdown body is the one value that cannot be read on one line, so a
row is the wrong shape for it, and putting it first in the canonical order pushes everything else
below the fold on any entry with an agenda in it. It keeps its place in the canonical order of
fields everywhere that order is a list of fields; it simply is not one of the rows.

**No editor writes to the repo.** The field popups write into the draft exactly as the inline
rows do, so the old rule that a sub-popup never writes is not a carve-out any more: nothing
below the top row's disk writes at all. **The body is the one field whose open shape still
carries a line of its own** — a textarea cannot have its name and its buttons beside it — and
that line is the same header the closed body already shows, so nothing moves there either. **That
header is the only name it carries**: the open body is the textarea and nothing else. A label
reading *Notes* under a header reading *Details* named the field twice, and a line explaining that
the box held raw markdown said what the monospace face already says. The group manager behind
*edit groups* is the one overlay here that does write, and it is not editing a field of an entry.

**Picking a category takes it.** Tapping a group puts it in the draft and closes the popup —
there is nothing more to say about a choice from a list, and with no save in it there is nothing
for a second tap to press.

### The title, the when, and the toggle row

**The title is a row too** — text until clicked, then an input in the same line at the same size.
So is **the when**, which reads `MON, 20.11.2026 · 09:00–10:00` and opens the start and end date
and time boxes in a popup under it. Four input boxes at the top of a popup opened to find out what
day something is on was the form at its least readable; four of them also cannot be a line, which
makes the when the clearest case for the popup — the row goes on reading the day while they are
open, and only takes the new reading once they are shut.

**The times are typed, not a native time control.** `HH:MM`, and forgiving about how it is reached:
`9` and `900` and `9:00` all read back as `09:00`, `930` and `0930` and `9:3` as `09:30`, and
anything that is not a time of day is refused and the box goes back to what the draft still holds.
A native `<input type="time">` takes its 12- or 24-hour shape from the device's locale and nothing
in markup, CSS or a `lang` attribute can tell it otherwise, while [every other time in the
calendar is 24-hour by construction](#the-filter-and-the-settings). **The two dates stay native**,
because a date picker is worth more than a format and a date, unlike a time, cannot be misread
into a different value.

The when-line no longer repeats the stage, the importance and the estimate as words. The toggle
row shows all three, live, directly beneath it.

### The toggle row

One row of icons directly under the when. These are not fields with an editor each: they are
small values, edited in the row itself with a single tap, and they **show their value** rather
than merely whether they have one — each as a small badge on the corner of its icon.

**A tap on one of them is the whole edit**, into the draft like everything else — there is
nothing in these four to type, so there is nothing for a row's `x` to put back and no editor to
open. The disk appears on the first tap, as it does for any other change.

- **`24h` for all-day** — the one control in the popup that is a word rather than a picture, and
  deliberately so: every drawing of a whole day reads as something else. The sun it replaces was
  taken for weather or for daylight hours, and `24h` cannot be. **A clickable control, not a
  checkbox** — lit when on, plain when off. On an event it is alone on the row. Only the button
  changes its name: the strip in the week and day grids still reads `all-day`, and so does this
  document, because the word is the clearer one in prose and the button is the one place with no
  room for it.
- three small columns for **stage** — cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, its badge in
  that stage's kanban colour: red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- a `!` for **important** — a straight toggle, lit when the task is important and plain when it
  is not. It carries no badge: a yes or no has nothing a badge could add that the lit state has
  not already said, which is what made the old flag need a digit and this one not.
- an hourglass for **estimate** — the one of the four that opens an editor, because a number has
  to be typed. It opens **in a popup under the hourglass**, so the toggle row keeps its one line
  like every other row. That popup is the one that carries the trashcan itself, because its row is
  an icon with no room beside it. Its badge reads the day count as `2d`.

## The filter, the settings and the logs

**One button, three errands, named before any opens.** The hamburger opens a short dropdown
reading `filter`, `settings` and `logs`, and opens none of them; a second tap opens the one that
was meant. One button still covers them all, so the pane stays at four controls and the phone's
first row does not gain a fifth — but the button no longer decides which of them you came for.

They were one panel for a while, under a heading each. A heading is a weak way to separate a thing
you open daily from a thing you open twice, and it cost the filter the room to show its groups:
the list had to be folded away or it pushed the nine settings rows below the fold. Naming the two
and opening them apart costs one tap and buys each of them its own shape.

**The filter is a dropdown off the hamburger.** It is the half you open often — a group hidden
this afternoon, the board narrowed to what is important — and the view it narrows has to stay in
sight while it is narrowed, which a centred card over the middle of the screen cannot do.

**The settings are a centred panel**, titled `Settings`, whose top right has an `x` to close.
They are the nine rows that change once, so they may take the middle of the screen.

**The logs are a centred panel too**, titled `Logs`, and they are the answer to a sync line that
says something unexpected. The line `14 change(s) pending` used to be the whole of what the app
would say about a queue that could not drain: the reason was written to that same line by
whichever push failed and overwritten by the next focus, so a browser could sit on a count it
could neither explain nor clear. The panel holds three things —

- **the state**, with `push now` and `discard all` beside it;
- **the last attempt**: whether it was a push or a pull, what it failed with, how many times in a
  row, and since when;
- **what is waiting**: one line per queued change — `put` or `del`, its path, and how long it has
  been there.

`push now` is the same drain the app runs on open and on focus, so the panel adds no second way
to sync. `discard all` is the one control in Mine that can lose work, so it confirms through the
browser's own prompt, the way *forget this device* does on the tile screen, rather than through
the calendar's discard prompt — whose **don't ask again** would switch this guard off along with
the one it belongs to. Discarding also forgets the local copy of every path it held and drops the
ETag, so the next pull restores exactly what GitHub holds; forgetting the queue alone would leave
text in the mirror that no later pull would ever reconcile.

**The sync line is a button.** It is what you are looking at when you want to know why it says
what it says, and reaching the panel through the hamburger only helps once you know the panel is
there.

| overlay | holds |
| --- | --- |
| Filter (a dropdown) | a checkbox per group; on the board also **important only** and an **assignee** |
| Settings (a centred panel) | the nine rows below |
| Logs (a centred panel) | the last sync attempt, the changes still queued, `push now`, `discard all` |

**The groups are listed, not folded behind a dropdown.** One checkbox per group, each showing its
colour, straight away — one tap to hide a group instead of two. The fold existed for one reason,
that an open list pushed the nine settings rows below the fold, and that reason went with the
settings. A repo with twenty groups scrolls inside the dropdown rather than growing it past the
screen. This is a view filter and is remembered per device; groups are *named and coloured* in the
settings panel's **edit groups**, not here.

**Times read 24-hour everywhere, and are typed that way.** The hour gutter in the week and day
grids, a time on a card, a time in a row — all `HH:MM`, with no setting to change it and no
12-hour form anywhere. There is no *time format* row beside *date format* because there is nothing
to choose. The one control that could have disagreed was the native time input in the when popup,
which took its shape from the device's locale; [it is a typed box
instead](#the-title-the-when-and-the-toggle-row).

**Every row is two halves: the label in the left half, its control in the right.** That one rule
is what the panel was missing. A select, a text box, a checkbox and a date field each began
wherever its own label happened to end, so nine tidy rows read as a ragged column — and the fix
is alignment, not fewer settings. The controls now line up in one column down the panel.

Nine rows, and the labels are short enough to fit their half on one line at 320 px — which is
why two of them are no longer named after the kanban:

| row | control |
| --- | --- |
| Groups | an **edit groups** button |
| Start week on | Monday or Sunday |
| Time zone | a zone name such as `Europe/Berlin`, defaulting to the device's own |
| Date format | `auto` (the device's locale), `dd.mm.yyyy` or `mm/dd/yy` |
| Calendar weeks | the month view's week-number gutter |
| Confirm discard | whether leaving an edited popup asks before discarding |
| Sprint length | in weeks |
| First sprint | the date sprint 1 starts on |

questions.question: You want the when-preview to read 'THU, 19.11.26 15:00'. But Mine has a device-wide Date format setting (auto / dd.mm.yyyy / mm/dd/yy) that every other date in the app obeys via formatDate(), and REQUIREMENTS.md argues the when-row reads 'MON, 20.11.2026 · 09:00–10:00' through it. A hard-coded DD.MM.YY would be the one date in Mine that ignores that setting. Which wins?

options.label: Short mode honouring the setting (Recommended)
options.description: Add a short form to formatDate: dd.mm.yyyy → 19.11.26, mm/dd/yy → 11/19/26, auto → the locale's 2-digit-year form. With your setting on dd.mm.yyyy you get exactly 19.11.26, and the setting keeps meaning something.

options.label: Hard-code DD.MM.YY
options.description: The when-preview always reads 19.11.26 regardless of the Date format setting. Exactly your spec, literally; the setting then governs every date except this one.

options.label: Keep 4-digit year, honour setting
options.description: 'THU, 19.11.2026 15:00' via the existing formatDate. Two extra characters per side, which matters since two of these now share one line.

options.description: THU on an English device, DO on a German one, dots stripped. Matches how the app already builds the day-view period label (weekdayName sliced + uppercased) and the week grid headers, so no second weekday convention appears.

options.label: Always 3-char English
options.description: MON TUE WED THU FRI SAT SUN, everywhere, whatever the device locale. Exactly your 'THU'; it's the only English-forced string in an otherwise locale-driven app.

content.text: Now the date/time flow — the largest item. Several questions in a row here.

questions.question: The flow you describe runs start date → start time → end date → end time. But most edits to an existing entry are 'this starts at 15:00, not 14:00' or 'it now runs to Saturday' — and walking four steps to change one of them is worse than today's four boxes. Where can the flow be entered?

options.label: Each half of the row is its own target (Recommended)
options.description: Tapping the start text starts at start-date and runs all four steps; tapping the end text starts at end-date and runs the last two. The multi-day row already has a left and a right half, so the targets are visible — and a single-day row's '15:00–17:00' splits at the dash the same way.

options.label: One target, always all four steps
options.description: Tapping anywhere on the row starts at start-date; every edit walks start date, start time, end date, end time. Exactly your spec, simplest to build and to document; four taps to fix an end time.

options.label: One target, each step skippable
options.description: Tapping anywhere starts at start-date, and each step has a 'next' that leaves the value alone — so reaching the end time is four taps but never destructive. Adds a button to every step.

questions.question: There is no time picker in the app today — times are typed, and REQUIREMENTS.md argues at length against native <input type="time"> because it takes 12h/24h shape from the device locale and nothing can override that. So 'switch to time picker' has to be something I build. What should it be?

options.label: Hour grid, then quarter-hours (Recommended)
options.description: Step one: 24 hour buttons (6×4, 00–23) with the current hour marked. Step two: :00 :15 :30 :45. Two taps, no scrolling, fits the anchored popup at 320px, 24h by construction. Anything else — 15:37 — is reached by typing digits, which jumps to the HH:MM box.

options.label: Scrollable list, 15-min steps
options.description: One column of 00:00–23:45 scrolled to the current value; one tap picks. Simpler to reason about, but it's 96 rows to scroll and the popup has no scrim, so a scroll gesture near its edge is a dismissal.

options.label: Just the HH:MM text box
options.description: Selecting a date advances to the typed HH:MM field — the one that already exists and already accepts 9, 900, 930. No picker to build, and the keyboard opens on a phone every time.

questions.question: The typed date box: you specified DD.MM.YYYY. We just agreed the preview honours the Date format setting, so a device set to mm/dd/yy would read '11/19/26' and then be asked to type '19.11.2026'. How should the typed box be ordered, and how lenient should it be?

options.label: Order follows the setting, lenient digits (Recommended)
options.description: dd.mm.yyyy → DD.MM.YYYY; mm/dd/yy → MM/DD/YYYY; auto → whichever order the locale puts first, derived from a probe date. Separators optional and either kind: 1911, 191126, 19112026 and 19.11.2026 all land on 19.11.2026 — the same forgiveness hhmm() already gives times. Rejects anything that isn't a date and the box falls back to the draft's value.

options.label: Always DD.MM.YYYY, lenient digits
options.description: Exactly your spec: one typed order everywhere, same leniency. A mm/dd/yy device reads dates one way and types them the other.

options.label: Always ISO YYYY-MM-DD
options.description: Matches the files on disk and the native date inputs the app uses elsewhere, and can never be misread. Nothing else the user sees is ISO, and it's the most keystrokes.

questions.question: The icons that collapse into the quick row are: 24h, stage, important, category (ball), repeat, alerts (bell) — six on a task, four on an event (no stage, no important). options.label: Flags, then fields: 24h · stage · ! · ball · repeat · bell (Recommended)
options.description: Keeps the reading order the popup has today — the toggle row sits above the field rows, and the expanded view will list them in exactly this order. An event simply loses the middle two and the row closes up.

options.label: Fields, then flags: ball · repeat · bell · 24h · stage · !
options.description: Leads with the canonical field order REQUIREMENTS.md states (category, repetition, alerts, location, participants), with the three small values after it. The event/task difference then falls at the end of the row.

options.label: Flags and fields split by a gap
options.description: 24h stage !   ball repeat bell — a visible gap saying the left three toggle in place and the right three open something. Costs width that the sixth icon needs on a 320px phone.

The category ball filled with the category's colour: `ball` is already a solid disc path, so this is colouring the svg. Two cases to settle — what the ball looks like with no category chosen, and what happens when a category's colour is nearly the popup's background (groups are user-chosen, so a near-white or near-black one is possible).

options.label: Ink when unset, plain fill when set (Recommended)
options.description: No category → the ball stays the row's ink colour like every other icon, so an unset row reads as unset. Set → the group's colour, flat, no ring — the same thing the filter's and the group manager's .swatch already does, and a group coloured like the background is a problem the user made and can see in three other places.

options.label: Ink when unset, fill + thin ring when set
options.description: A 1px ring in the row's ink colour around the filled disc, so any colour stays visible against any background. It's a drawing no other swatch in Mine has, so the ball and the swatch stop matching.

options.label: Grey when unset
options.description: Unset uses the same #9aa5b1 that colorOf() returns for an unknown group, so the ball is always a coloured disc. A deliberately grey category then looks exactly like no category.

questions.question: Files in mine-data carry `estimate: 3`. The popup's FORM_KEYS list says which keys the form owns — those get cleared and rewritten on save, and TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md states everything else (exdate, status, hand-added keys) survives a save untouched. Once the UI no longer has an estimate, what should a save do with an existing one?

options.label: Leave it alone — it becomes a foreign key (Recommended)
options.description: `estimate` comes out of FORM_KEYS, so a file that has one keeps it through any number of edits, exactly as a hand-added key does. The app stops reading, showing and writing it; nothing of yours is deleted by a save you made for another reason. Your old estimates stay greppable in the repo until you remove them yourself.

options.label: Dropped on the next save
options.description: `estimate` stays in FORM_KEYS and is never written back, so editing an entry quietly strips it. 'Removed completely' in the strongest sense; it makes a save that touched a title delete data, which is the one thing the FORM_KEYS rule exists to prevent.

options.description: A pass that rewrites every file carrying an estimate, in one commit, then the key is gone everywhere. Hundreds of files in one push, and it's a migration tool nothing else in Mine has.

'Continued top row elements' can be built two ways, and they differ a lot in cost. The month view is a flat CSS grid of 42 independent day cells, each with its own stack of entry lines and its own '+N' cap; the week/day view has an all-day strip of one cell per column. True spanning needs a band laid over each week row with lane packing so overlapping spans don't collide.

options.label: A copy on each covered day, marked as continuing (Recommended)
options.description: The entry appears in the all-day strip / the top of each day cell it covers, flat-edged on the sides where it continues and rounded where it starts and ends, so a run of cells reads as one bar. The title is readable on every day — which matters on a phone, where a true bar shows its title only in the first column. Keeps the cell structure, the cap and the click handling exactly as they are.

options.label: True spanning bars with lane packing
options.description: One element per entry, spanning its columns, in a band above each week row and across the all-day strip, with lanes assigned so overlapping spans stack. Looks like Google Calendar; it's a rewrite of the month view's DOM and CSS, a new layout algorithm, and the '+N' cap has to be rethought against a band of variable height.

options.label: Spanning in week/day, copies in month
options.description: The all-day strip is a 7-column grid where a span is one grid-column rule, so spanning is nearly free there; the month view takes copies. Two renderings of one concept, and the month view is the one where multi-day entries are most often seen.

questions.question: Model shape for spans. Today `occurrences(model, from, to)` returns one occurrence per entry, keyed by path, with a single `dayKey` taken from the start — and it drops anything whose start day is outside the range, so a trip that began last month is invisible in this one. Two ways to fix it:

options.label: One occurrence per entry, views expand it (Recommended)
options.description: The occurrence gains `endDayKey`; the range test becomes an overlap test (start ≤ to and endDay ≥ from), and the rrule window widens by the series duration so a recurring span that began before the range is caught. views.js groups by covered day instead of by start day. The kanban keeps exactly one card per task, S.visible stays keyed by path, and overrides and clicks are untouched.

options.label: One occurrence per covered day
options.description: occurrences() emits a copy per day, each flagged first/last, so every view's day grouping works unchanged. But a 3-day task becomes three kanban cards unless the board dedupes, S.visible needs a composite key, and byStart/byImportance sort over duplicates.

options.label: A separate spans query
options.description: Leave occurrences() alone and add a second function the views call for spans only. Two range queries with two filter paths; the group filter, the new stage filter and the override logic all have to be applied in both.

content.text: Good — that's a scope addition: `important` becomes an event field too. Pinning its reach:

questions.question: Making `important` an event field as well touches a few places. Today it's task-only in three: data.js (`important: type === 'task' ? importantOf(data) : false`), the popup (the `!` appears only on a task), and TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md's table ('task only'). Nothing in any grid shows importance at all — it's visible only in the popup, on a kanban card's `!` prefix, and through the filter. How far does it go?

options.label: Field + popup + filter, no new markers (Recommended)
options.description: An event can be marked important, the `!` is in its icon row and its expanded line, the filter's important-only keeps it, and the docs move `important` to 'both'. No grid or preview gains an importance marker — an important task has none today either, so nothing new is invented and the two types stay consistent.

options.label: Also mark important entries in the views
options.description: An important entry gets a `!` on its line in the month cells, the time grids and the day preview, the way a kanban card already does. Importance becomes visible without opening anything; it costs characters in the one place they're scarcest (a month cell on a phone shows the title alone).

options.label: Field + filter only, keep `!` out of the event popup
options.description: Events can carry the key and the filter honours it, but only a task's popup can set it. Then an important event can only be made by hand in the file.

The board calls the same collect(sprintStart, sprintEnd); once that returns overlapping entries, a task that started in sprint 7 and ends in sprint 8 appears on **both** boards. But REQUIREMENTS.md and TECHNICAL-REQUIREMENTS.md both state a task's sprint is whichever range its **start** falls in, 'so the number can never contradict the date'.

options.label: Board stays start-based (Recommended)
options.description: renderKanban filters to tasks whose start day is inside the sprint, so a long task sits on exactly one board — the documented rule survives untouched and a card can't be moved from a sprint it doesn't belong to. The calendar views get spans; the board doesn't need them, since a card carries its date as text.

options.label: Board shows every overlapping task
options.description: A task spanning the boundary appears on both sprints' boards. Arguably truer to 'what am I working on this sprint'; it breaks the rule that a card's sprint is derived from its start, and dragging the same card on two boards writes two different dates.

options.label: Board shows overlaps, marked as carried over
options.description: Overlapping tasks appear on later boards with a continuation mark, as the grids do. A third rendering concept for the board, and the sprint/start rule still needs rewriting.

content.text:
We're aligned. Here's the spec I'll build from — ten commits, each with code + REQUIREMENTS prose + TEST-REQUIREMENTS entry + `check-calendar.mjs` assertions, `test/run.sh` green and screenshots inspected before the next starts.

## Agreed decisions

**1 · Remove the estimate** — gone from `popup.js` (EST, `estimateEditor`, `estBtn`, the `estimate` draft field, `snapshot`), `data.js` (`estimateOf`, `occurrence.estimate`), the `glass` icon, the CSS, the sample file and its prose, both docs, TEST-REQUIREMENTS and the suite. `estimate` comes **out of FORM_KEYS**, so a file that has one keeps it through any save, as a hand-added key does. mine-data is yours; nothing breaks if you never touch it.

**2 · Shared month picker** — the day-grid drawing comes out of `app.js` into `calendar/ui.js` as `monthPicker({value, highlight, onPick})`; the top bar, the when-flow and the repeat end-date all call it. Year and sprint modes stay in `app.js`.

**3 · The when row** — `formatDate` gains a short form honouring the Date format setting (`dd.mm.yyyy` → `19.11.26`), weekday is the locale short name uppercased (`THU`, `DO`). Single day: `THU, 19.11.26 15:00–17:00`. Multi-day: start left, end right, wrapping to a second right-aligned line when it doesn't fit. All-day prints no time; no end prints no dash; no date reads `no date`.

Each half is a target. Start half → **start date → start time → end date → end time**; end half → the last two, always entering at the end *date*. All-day skips both time steps. Walking it always sets an end (seeded start +1h). Time picker: 24 hour buttons, then `:00 :15 :30 :45`. Typing a digit in any step jumps to a text box — date ordered by your Date format setting and lenient (`1911`, `191126`, `19112026`, `19.11.2026`), Enter advances. Head reads the step name with a `‹` back on every step but the first; x / Escape / outside tap leave and keep what committed. An end before the start is silently clamped to the start.

**4 · Two coloured icons** — the category ball fills with the group's colour when set, stays ink when unset, no ring. Stage reuses the `check` tick-in-square, filled red/yellow/green with the tick knocked out; the corner badge and the `cols` icon go.

**5 · Icon row + expand** — `24h · stage · ! · ball · repeat · bell` (events lose stage), set fields read lit, hover/aria carry the value. A chevron at the row's right end; expanded, the rows appear *beneath* the icon row, state remembered as `calendar.popupExpanded`. 24h and important toggle in place in both views; stage cycles in both, its line reading `Doing`. The expanded view is lines only: a two-chip `[24h] All-day  [!] Important` line, then stage, category, repeat, alerts, location, participants, details. Category's picker head gains the red trashcan (the old `popClear`) so it can be cleared from the icon row.

**6 · Alerts** — single-valued anchored list: `none · at start · 5 min before · 15 min before · 1 hour before · 1 day before`, stored as a one-item list. A file with `0, 15` or a lone `30` shows a non-selectable `custom · 0, 15` and is written back untouched until you pick.

**7 · Repeat** — tapping it drops the seven choices straight under the row (anchored list, like category), then always a second step for the end: `never` / `on a date` / `after n times`, current values marked, `‹` back. A date goes to the month picker; typing a digit jumps to the date box. `does not repeat` ends there. Custom rules stay non-selectable and preserved.

**8 · `important` on events** — field, popup `!`, filter and docs (`both`). No importance markers added to any grid.

**9 · Multi-day spans** — occurrence gains `endDayKey`; the range test becomes an overlap test and the rrule window widens by the series duration. All-day `end` is **inclusive** (the last day) — documented as a deliberate divergence, with a note that `.ics` export must add a day. Views render a copy per covered day in the top row, flat-edged where it continues and rounded at the ends. Timed spans leave the hour grid for the top strip (`15:00 Trip` / `Trip` / `→17:00 Trip`). The board stays **start-based**, so a card sits on one sprint only.

**10 · Filter + badge** — three stage checkboxes and an important switch in every view, applied in `collect()`, stored as `calendar.hiddenStages` / `calendar.importantOnly`. Stage never hides an event; important-only keeps only entries marked important, events included. The hamburger carries a circled count of active filter *kinds* (groups / stages / important / assignee), max 4, hidden at zero.

## Assumptions I did not ask about — say if any is wrong

- A span counts against the month cell's 2/4-line cap on each covered day, and sits at the top of the cell (all-day already sorts first).
- The day preview becomes span-aware: it lists entries covering that day, not entries starting on it.
- The year view needs no work — covered days take the group colour once the model expands.
- The all-day strip's `all-day` caption becomes a bare corner, since timed spans now ride it; the REQUIREMENTS line about the strip still saying "all-day" is rewritten.
- A multi-day *task* spans the grids exactly like an event.
- New-task defaults become `todo` and nothing else (the "estimate of 1 day" default and its paragraph go).

Say go and I'll start with the estimate removal.

A task carries the two keys an event never has: `stage` and `important`.

- `stage` is `todo`, `doing` or `done` and is the only record of progress - there is no
  `done` flag.

in, so the number can never disagree with the date, and moving the card to another sprint is
exactly a change of `start`. With the anchor and interval in `sample/settings.md` this one is
in sprint 8, 13-26 April 2026.

content.content:
No `duration` key — it is `end - start`.

There is no `priority` key. It was RFC 5545 `PRIORITY` and a scale of 1 to 3; importance is a
yes or no, so the scale had nothing to say. A file carrying one is not read for it, and the key
goes the next time the entry is saved, along with anything else the form does not own.

Type and time are independent: `type` decides whether the entry has a stage, an important mark
and an estimate, the value type of `start` decides whether it is all-day or timed. A task is
usually all-day, but may carry a time and then renders at it.

`stage` is a task's only progress field; there is no `done` key. A `stage` that is absent or is
not one of the three reads as `todo`.

`status` is deliberately *not* the stage field. It already means cancellation on an override,
and one key cannot carry both without an override's cancellation reading as a kanban column.

=== REQ 250-260
```

The top row carries **the type**, then right-aligned a trashcan to delete the entry, the disk
once there is something to save, and an `x` to close. On an entry that already exists the type is
a **marker, not a choice** — a ticked square for a task, a calendar page for an event, shown and
not pressable — because a task turned into an event drops its stage, its importance and its
estimate, and the type is settled when the entry is made. On a new entry it is the pair, with the
event selected. On a repeating one the **scope pair** follows the marker, left of the gap —
described below.

The trashcan stays at the left of that group: deleting is not an edit of a field, it writes at
=== REQ 300-312
  in the corner it is in everywhere in Mine. **The title row is the one with neither**, because an
  entry must have a title and so there is nothing to clear, and because the popup's own `x`, which
  discards the whole edit, is a thumb's width above that line; it closes on Escape or by opening
  any other row.
- **A field whose control cannot fit a line opens it in a popup anchored to the row.** The when,
  the category, the repetition and the estimate: four date and time boxes, a list of categories, a
  rule with an end condition, a number with a unit. The row keeps its icon, its value and its
  trashcan — **nothing about it moves** — and the popup hangs directly under it, naming the field
  and carrying an `x`. The estimate's is the one that also carries the trashcan, because its row
  is an icon on the toggle row with no room beside it.
- **The field popup carries no scrim**, alone among the calendar's overlays. A scrim would stop
  the tap that dismisses it, so moving from one field to the next would take two taps; without one
  the tap reaches the row it landed on and opens it. Tapping the row it is already on closes it
=== REQ 383-420
calendar is 24-hour by construction](#the-filter-and-the-settings). **The two dates stay native**,
because a date picker is worth more than a format and a date, unlike a time, cannot be misread
into a different value.

The when-line no longer repeats the stage, the importance and the estimate as words. The toggle
row shows all three, live, directly beneath it.

### The toggle row

One row of icons directly under the when. These are not fields with an editor each: they are
small values, edited in the row itself with a single tap, and they **show their value** rather
than merely whether they have one — each as a small badge on the corner of its icon.

**A tap on one of them is the whole edit**, into the draft like everything else — there is
nothing in these four to type, so there is nothing for a row's `x` to put back and no editor to
open. The disk appears on the first tap, as it does for any other change.

- **`24h` for all-day** — the one control in the popup that is a word rather than a picture, and
  deliberately so: every drawing of a whole day reads as something else. The sun it replaces was
  taken for weather or for daylight hours, and `24h` cannot be. **A clickable control, not a
  checkbox** — lit when on, plain when off. On an event it is alone on the row. Only the button
  changes its name: the strip in the week and day grids still reads `all-day`, and so does this
  document, because the word is the clearer one in prose and the button is the one place with no
  room for it.
- three small columns for **stage** — cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, its badge in
  that stage's kanban colour: red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- a `!` for **important** — a straight toggle, lit when the task is important and plain when it
  is not. It carries no badge: a yes or no has nothing a badge could add that the lit state has
  not already said, which is what made the old flag need a digit and this one not.
- an hourglass for **estimate** — the one of the four that opens an editor, because a number has
  to be typed. It opens **in a popup under the hourglass**, so the toggle row keeps its one line
  like every other row. That popup is the one that carries the trashcan itself, because its row is
  an icon with no room beside it. Its badge reads the day count as `2d`.

On an event, stage, important and estimate are not there at all, because an event has none of
them. They sit here so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban
card edits.

=== REQ 616-628
  phone the row also carries `<` `>`** to move the card to the previous or next stage — `<`

  there and the card is dragged between them, so arrows on every card are a second way to do what
  the drag already does, in the one place they are also easiest to mistake for the header's pager;
- below it two lines of the markdown body, and the day the task sits on.

title and two lines — the three things worth reading at a glance across three columns.

content.content:
live, directly beneath it.

### The toggle row

One row of icons directly under the when. These are not fields with an editor each: they are
small values, edited in the row itself with a single tap, and they **show their value** rather
than merely whether they have one — each as a small badge on the corner of its icon.

**A tap on one of them is the whole edit**, into the draft like everything else — there is
nothing in these three to type, so there is nothing for a row's `x` to put back and no editor to
open. The disk appears on the first tap, as it does for any other change.

- **`24h` for all-day** — the one control in the popup that is a word rather than a picture, and
  deliberately so: every drawing of a whole day reads as something else. The sun it replaces was
  taken for weather or for daylight hours, and `24h` cannot be. **A clickable control, not a
  checkbox** — lit when on, plain when off. On an event it is alone on the row. Only the button
  changes its name: the strip in the week and day grids still reads `all-day`, and so does this
  document, because the word is the clearer one in prose and the button is the one place with no
  room for it.
- three small columns for **stage** — cycles `todo` → `doing` → `done` on each tap, its badge in
  that stage's kanban colour: red, yellow, green. There is no stage popup.
- a `!` for **important** — a straight toggle, lit when the task is important and plain when it
  is not. It carries no badge: a yes or no has nothing a badge could add that the lit state has
  not already said, which is what made the old flag need a digit and this one not.
On an event, stage and important are not there at all, because an event has neither. They sit
here so that a task that is not on a board still carries the two fields a kanban card edits.

Neither lit control — `24h` or `!` — is the disk's green: in all of Mine green is a save and red
is a trashcan, and a green toggle beside the disk would make the popup look like it offers two
primary actions.

— with all three on the input's own line and the `x` rightmost, resolved from their top edges and
left edges. That **the title row carries neither**, the popup's own `x` being a thumb's width
above it. That the row's `x` **closes the row and keeps what is in it**, and still writes nothing.
That clicking a second row closes the first the same way.

For the when, the category, the repetition and the estimate: that clicking it opens `#fpop`
**under the row**, that the row's height, its text and the number of rows in the popup are all
unchanged, that the row holds no control of its own, and that **no scrim is raised** — the tap
that dismisses this popup has to reach the row it landed on. That tapping a different row moves
straight to it in **one tap**, and that tapping the row it is already on **closes** it rather than
reopening it. That `#fpop`'s own `x` closes it and leaves the entry popup open. That no `#sub`
popup is opened by any of the nine.

That only one is open at a time, an inline input and a field popup never both. That **Escape is
swallowed by a field popup and not by an inline row**: in a field popup it closes that and leaves
the entry popup open, and in an inline row it asks the discard question, the row staying as it is.
A new entry opens with its title row already an input, so a row that swallowed Escape would cost
two presses to leave the commonest popup in the app.

**One edit is one commit.** That editing four things in one popup and pressing the disk queues
**one** write, and that the file then holds all four values. This is the measurement a popup
writing per row could not pass, and it is the reason for the draft, so it is checked as a count
and not only as an outcome.

**The trashcan on a row.** That a set row carries one and an unset row does not, and that the
estimate's lives in its popup's head instead, its row being an icon with no room beside it. That
it clears the field in the draft — the row drops to its muted name and the disk appears — and that it does
**not** write on its own. That **clicking a row's trashcan does not activate the row**: the field
is cleared and no input appears, which is the same rule a kanban card holds to and matters more
here, the trashcan now being on the surface being tapped.

That a ticked checkbox is not pressable. That the body is **rendered and shown in full** when the
row is inactive — the whole text, not a clipped line — and that clicking it replaces the rendered
nodes with a textarea holding the raw markdown, with its `x` at the foot.

**The toggle row.** That a new entry is an event and its toggle row holds `24h` by itself; that
choosing a task puts stage, important and estimate on that same row and switching back to an
event takes all three away again. That stage cycles through three stages in three badge colours
and back; that **important is a toggle and not a cycle** — two taps return it to where it started,
it carries no badge and no digit, and there is no third state to reach; and that the estimate
opens its editor **in a popup under the hourglass**, leaving the toggle row's own height and row
count untouched, prefilled with one day, badges `3d` once set and
loses its badge once cleared. That a tap on any of the four **changes the draft and not the
repo**: the disk appears, the queue stays empty. That `24h` and `!` light with the ordinary
enabled background and never with `--good`, because green is the disk's, and that nothing else in
the popup lights at all. That the row sits **below** the when row, not above it — resolved from
the same — the pane narrowing with the board is the failure mode of capping `#cal` instead of the
board, and it is invisible until the two widths are compared.

**What a card holds, and what it no longer holds.** That a card's top row is the title alone,
with a `!` in front of it when the task is important and nothing in front of it when not; that
the `!` is **not a button** — no element bearing it is pressable; and that the card carries **no
pen, no trashcan, no estimate, no sprint number and no priority chip** — and there is no pen
anywhere in the calendar to find. On a desktop the card
holds no pressable element at all, and on a phone only the two stage arrows: the count is what
keeps the removed controls removed, since each of them came back once as a chip.

**Clicking a control on a card does not open the ticket.** That tapping the phone's `<` or `>`
moves the card and leaves the entry popup closed, and that clicking the card's body does open it,
with no input element in it until a row is clicked.
This is the check for the bug where the board's own click delegation matched the card from inside
one of its buttons, so both happened at once; it must be written so that a handler that stops at
the button but lets the event bubble turns it red.

**A save is green and a trashcan is red**, in the popup's top row, on a field row, and in the
groups popup — no longer on a kanban card, which has no trashcan to colour. The check resolves
`--good`
and `--bad` from the page rather than naming colours, so retheming does not break it. Both are
**glyphs**: the save's `--good` must be its text colour and its background must be transparent.
A filled green button anywhere in Mine is a failure, so the check reads the background as well as
the colour — that is the half of it that
can catch a regression to the old style.

**What a saved task writes.** A new task saved with nothing but a title must land as
`stage: todo` with `estimate: 1`, and a task whose estimate was cleared must have no `estimate`
key at all — not an empty one, and never `None`. The same holds for importance: a task marked
important writes `important: true`, an unmarked one writes **no `important` key**, and no file
ever gains `important: false`. That a file carrying `important: true` reaches the toggle row lit
and one without the key does not. There is no `priority` and no `done` to read any more, and

content.content:
Take the prefix off pull(), and write down how to add an app

pull(prefix) filtered the tree by prefix but stored the single repo-wide commitEtag
regardless. A diary calling pull('diary/') would have stored the ETag of a commit it had
not mirrored, and the calendar's next pull would 304 against it and never see its own
files again. No caller ever passed one - and it was precisely the parameter a second app
would have reached for first. A per-folder pull needs a per-folder ETag, and what it
saves is one conditional GET.

index.html, the one entry in shared/apps.js, the VERSION bump, and the test suite - plus
what is already done for you, which is now most of it.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'MSG' && git log --oneline -1
Take the estimate out

A task carried an estimate in days, and nothing ever read it: it was shown in the popup
that set it and nowhere else, so it was a number to keep up to date rather than one to
act on. The field, its hourglass, its default of one day and its badge are gone, and
with them the one field popup that carried its own trashcan.

`estimate` comes **out of FORM_KEYS**, so it is now a key the form does not own: a file
that still carries one keeps it through any number of saves, exactly as a hand-added key
does. Nothing in this repo writes or reads one again - dropping it out of ORDER means a
preserved estimate serialises after the keys the form does own, which is where every
other foreign key already lands.

The sample task's body described three task keys and now describes two. The suite loses
the hourglass checks and gains the opposite one: a saved task must carry no `estimate`
key at all, not even the default it used to be given.
